**Xerox — the scanner that quietly changed the numbers on a building plan (2013)**

In 2013 the computer scientist David Kriesel scanned a set of construction plans on a Xerox WorkCentre copier and noticed something that should not be possible: room dimensions in the scan did not match the paper on his desk. Digits had changed. A 6 came out as an 8. The paper original was correct; the file was wrong.

Kriesel published his findings and reproduced the fault on six WorkCentre models and two machines from Xerox's ColorQube range; The Register and others covered it. The cause was the compression the machines used to shrink scanned PDFs. JBIG2 works by building a dictionary of small image patches: where two patches look similar enough by its measure, it stores one and reuses it in place of the other. On a page of printed digits, the block of pixels forming a 6 and the block forming an 8 can score as near-identical. The scanner did not misread the number — it never read the number at all. It swapped one rectangle of pixel values for another, and the digit changed as a side effect.

That is what makes it unnerving. There is no smudge, no garbled character, no warning: the output looks like a crisp, confident scan, and it says something the original did not.

This is the lesson's point pushed to its conclusion. An image is not a picture the machine understands; it is a grid of numbers, and everything done to it — compressing, brightening, converting to grey — is arithmetic on those numbers. Once you hold that idea, you can ask the right question of any tool in your pipeline: what exactly did it do to my array, and could the change be invisible to the eye but fatal to the meaning?

**Interpol — the face hidden by a twist, recovered by untwisting it (2007)**

For three years investigators held a set of photographs showing a man abusing children in south-east Asia. The offender's face had been digitally obscured with a swirl: the pixels around a centre point rotated, the twist growing toward the middle, so the features smeared into a spiral. With no face, there was no suspect.

A swirl, though, is not paint over a photograph. It is a rule that maps every pixel coordinate to a new coordinate — rotate this point about the centre, and make the angle larger the nearer it sits to that centre. That is the rotation matrix from this lesson, applied with a different angle at each radius. A mapping you can write down can be run backwards: rotate each pixel by the same angle in the opposite direction and the original arrangement reappears. Working with German police computer specialists, Interpol reversed the twist. In October 2007 it published the image in a global public appeal, Operation Vico, which it described as the first of its kind. Tips arrived from around the world, and Thai police arrested Christopher Paul Neil eleven days after the appeal launched; he was later convicted and jailed.

Two ideas from this lesson did that work. First, a geometric transform moves coordinates, not content — nothing had been destroyed, only relocated. Second, these transforms are invertible, because a matrix that rotates by an angle has a partner that rotates by minus that angle.

Hold on to that when you rotate, scale and flip images in the exercises. You are not editing pixels. You are choosing where each one goes — and anyone who works out the rule can send them back.

**LIGO — a signal pulled out of noise by sliding templates across it (2015–2016)**

On 14 September 2015 the two LIGO detectors recorded the first direct observation of a gravitational wave — a ripple in spacetime from two merging black holes. What the instruments store is a stream of numbers: how much each detector's arms stretched and squeezed, thousands of times a second. The event lasted a fraction of a second and was quieter than the instrument's own noise. Read the raw numbers and you would see nothing.

The method that found it is the operation in this lesson. LIGO's search used matched filtering: take a short template — the numbers a given pair of merging masses ought to produce — slide it along the data one sample at a time, and at each position multiply template against data and add up the products. Where the data does not resemble the template the products scatter and cancel toward zero; where it does, they reinforce and the sum spikes. That is a dot product at every position, the sliding-and-summing you are learning here. Because nobody knew the masses in advance, the collaboration slid a bank of about 250,000 templates across the data. The search reported a combined matched-filter signal-to-noise ratio of 24 and a false alarm rate estimated below one event in 203,000 years.

The spike came from arithmetic alone: multiply, add, step along, repeat.

Your kernel [-1, 1] on the row [10, 10, 20, 20] is that same operation on a smaller stage. The weights state what pattern you are hunting — a difference, an average, a black-hole merger — and the sliding sum reports where the data agrees. Change the numbers in the kernel and you change what the image will tell you.

**Duke University — rows shifted by one, and the model recommended the wrong drug (2006–2011)**

In 2006 a team at Duke University published work in Nature Medicine claiming that a genomic signature read from a patient's tumour could predict which chemotherapy would work. Duke opened clinical trials that used those signatures to assign real patients to treatments.

When the statisticians Keith Baggerly and Kevin Coombes at MD Anderson Cancer Center tried to reproduce the analysis, they could not. Working backwards from the data — an exercise they called forensic bioinformatics, written up in the Annals of Applied Statistics in 2009 — they found errors of exactly the kind this lesson warns about. Rows of the gene-expression matrix were shifted by one against their labels, so measurements were attributed to the wrong genes: an off-by-one. Elsewhere the sensitive and resistant labels were reversed, inverting the model's recommendation. Nothing crashed. Every array had a valid shape and every number was plausible. The output looked like an answer. Duke suspended the trials and papers were retracted; the episode was later reviewed by the Institute of Medicine and covered by The Cancer Letter and 60 Minutes.

That is the real shape of danger in array work. The uint8 overflow in this lesson is the friendly version: 200 plus 100 becomes 44, the image visibly darkens, and you know at once. The dangerous version stays plausible — a crop slipped by a row, a channel read as red that was blue, a label list no longer aligned with the array it describes.

Printing `img.shape` and `img.dtype` costs you nothing. Print them, and check that row 0 really is what you believe row 0 to be.

**Toyota — an access key left in a public repository for five years (2017–2022)**

In December 2017 a subcontractor working on the website for Toyota's T-Connect connected-car service uploaded part of the source code to a personal repository. The repository was public. Inside that code sat an access key to a data server.

The mistake came to light in September 2022, nearly five years later. Toyota's disclosure, reported by The Register, Computer Weekly and others, said the exposed key could be used to reach a server holding the email addresses and customer management numbers of 296,019 people registered for T-Connect. Toyota made the repository private on discovery and changed the key two days afterwards, but it could not rule out that the data had been read, so it notified everyone affected.

Note what the fix could not do. Making the repository private removed it from view; it did not remove the key from the commit history, and it could not un-see what anyone had already copied. Once a secret has been pushed to a public remote, it is compromised. The only real remedy is to rotate it.

This is why the short list of what never goes into Git is not housekeeping. A `.gitignore` is a habit you build before you need it — on your first small project, when the only thing at stake is a stray `.venv` folder or a dataset that makes the repository slow to clone. Build the habit while it is cheap and it will be automatic later, when the file you nearly commit holds an API key. And if you do slip, do not quietly delete the line and carry on. Rotate the key.
